issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Rafael had spent most of his life working as a welder, a man who understood heat, pressure, and the necessity of keeping a steady hand even when metal hissed and sparked. Since his wife died, he lived alone and kept to a narrow routine, but the panic that brought him to treatment began much earlier, in the period after he was tortured during a time of political violence in his home country. He described being taken to a confined room with armed men, nowhere to go and no way to control what happened next. The memory he carried from that time was not a clean story with a beginning and an end; when he tried to speak about it, he lost the thread, his account broke apart, and he would stop mid-sentence as if he had stepped back into the room. What remained most vivid was the feeling that it was happening right now, not decades ago, and the rush of rage that came every time he let himself remember.

Certain moments still pulled him straight back. The slam of a metal door, the sudden crack of a gunshot on television, or even a sharp noise from the street could make his body go rigid, because those sounds seemed to announce that violence was near and that he had no options. A crowded doorway at the grocery store or a repair bay where he could not easily leave could have the same effect. In those moments, Rafael's mind did not stay in the present; it folded into the old scene, and the torture felt immediate again. That sense of being trapped made the old memory flare, and once it did, the world around him narrowed to the possibility of harm. He became convinced that if he did not stay alert, violence could arrive from anywhere, and that fear colored the places and people around him as potentially dangerous.

As the years passed, Rafael tried to manage these surges in the only ways that seemed available to him. When the memory surged, he detached himself from it, pushing it away as if it belonged to someone else. He tried hard not to think about the torture at all, and when he felt threatened he became overly compliant, quick to agree, quick to apologize, quick to smooth over tension before it could grow. He had come to believe that you can never know who will harm you, and that belief kept him watching for danger in everyday life. It also deepened his self-blame. He told himself that the event happened because of the way he acted, and that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. Those thoughts made the old fear feel justified, and they also made him more likely to fall silent, to yield, and to keep his distance from anything that might stir up what he called "that room."

The cycle became especially visible at work, where the welding shop itself could turn into a place of repeated reminders. A loud bang from a nearby machine, a burst of sparks, or the sudden clatter of dropped steel could bring back the same trapped feeling that had followed him for years. After those moments, Rafael would withdraw into himself, refuse to talk about what had happened, and focus only on getting through the shift without drawing attention. He noticed that he started to avoid certain tasks that required him to work in tighter spaces, and he would linger near exits when he could. The more he tried not to think about the torture, the more the memories seemed to ambush him, and the more he felt he had to watch for danger. That vigilance did not ease his fear; it kept the world arranged around threat, and it made every sudden sound or constricted space feel like proof that harm could return at any moment.

By the time he sought help, Rafael was exhausted by how often the past would seize him and by how much of his life had shrunk around that fear. He wanted relief from the way the memory arrived as if it were happening now, and from the anger and self-accusation that followed. What finally brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep living as though every unexpected noise or blocked doorway meant violence was about to begin. He was most afraid that his body would keep reacting before his mind could catch up, and most hoping that someone might help him believe, even a little, that the danger was not always around the corner.
